newsitem.title: ITALY: Armani jokes about fashion in film about style.
newsitem.headline: Armani jokes about fashion in film about style.

text.p: Italy's design king Giorgio Armani played jester to himself and the fashion world on Thursday when he prefaced his Emporio collection with a short film about a Hollywood Cinderella saved -- sartorially -- by Armani style.

The film "Salvation", starring actress Jennifer Tilly and directed by David La Chapelle, shows a sorry-looking news-stand girl with a disastrous haircut and a fluorescent green top under verbal and physical attack from a bizarre train of customers.

Her stall ransacked and her world in tatters, Tilly lies juddering in the gutter before the "Salvation Armani" arrive and she is sartorially resurrected as a starlet -- haircut and all -- by men in white coats.

With Tilly, nominated for an Academy Award in Woody Allen's "Bullets over Broadway", settled in the audience next to the silver-haired stylist's catwalk, the designer got down to the more serious business of unveiling his spring/summer 1997 Emporio Armani collection.
Unlike the news-stand vendor's screaming green, the ready-to-wear line-up consisted of the more demure hues of navy, black and golden beige. The overall silhouette was long, slender and fluid.
"Emporio Armani proposes a way of being sophisticated that finds a source in the chic exoticism of the Twenties, without giving in to complacent nostalgia," the designer said.

The collection included long shirt-jackets to the calf, cut away from the body or long and narrow in the style of Indian soldiers, minimalist rounded collars on straight jackets and the occasional twist of a monochrome scarf knotted at the neck.

A hint of the Orient pervaded the collection with transparent Japanese sandals as footwear, bands worn dashingly across the chest, and long straight tunics over narrow transparent pants or slender ivory leggings under long see-through slitted skirts.

There was no stinting on material, with generous lengths to caftan style dresses. In one design the model was enveloped to the floor in simple folds of rich dark grey silk topped off by a dark stole clasped about the shoulders.

Evening wear also included glittering sequinned tops and jackets of delicate green and pink like the interior of a seashell as well as transparent blue or green full-length gowns with regular polka dots.
For leisure came a collection of black-on-white and white-on-black bathing suits, shorts and beachwear for women and men.
Design house Missoni, in a show earlier on Thursday, evoked luxuriously hot tropics and cooling sea water in a rainbow display of ready-to-wear designs.

Calling the collection "Water Follies", Missoni cited sunsets and rain forests as the inspiration behind the cocktail of violet, aquamarine, red and ochre laid side by side in zig-zag wave patterns and irregular diagonal stripes.

Hems brushed ankles or skimmed the floor giving an elegant and fluid silhouette and exuding an air of languid, comfortable sophistication, rendered more casual for beachwear when models padded down the catwalk barefoot.

For evening, models wore sequinned full-length gowns or tunics and camisole tops and trousers in violet, red and yellow horizontal stripes, some tied at the waist, others low backed, as well as similar styles solely in purple or pink.
Daywear included straight wraparound skirts, long shifts and towelling tops while footwear was either high-heeled elegance or simple flat sandals.
Fashion house Gucci parades its designs late on Thursday and the shows end on Sunday with Armani's main Giorgio Armani line.
